Pedir informação e resolver trâmites no: Asking for information and getting things done at the bank
AVISO: o que o banco pede a um estrangei: NOTE: what a bank asks of a foreigner, its fees and its deadlines vary by country, bank and time. Here you learn how to ask for and understand the information; always check the facts in current sources. STEP 1: to ask for something politely, use «quisiera» or «me gustaría» + infinitive, with no preposition: «Quisiera abrir una cuenta.» (I'd like to open an account.) STEP 2: to find out what's needed, ask «¿Qué necesito para…?» or «¿Qué documentos hacen falta?» (What documents do I need?). «Hacer falta» agrees with what is needed: «Hace falta un documento» (singular), «Hacen falta dos documentos» (plural). With a verb, it stays singular: «Hace falta presentar un justificante». STEP 3: the information usually comes with impersonal «se» (lesson 49): «Se necesita un documento de identidad», «Se puede pagar con tarjeta». STEP 4: to ask about costs without assuming anything, use «¿Cobran comisión por…?» or «¿Tiene alguna comisión?». «Comisión» here is a bank fee, not a sales commission. STEP 5: to ask someone else to do something, use «quiero que» + subjunctive (lesson 43): «Quiero que me expliquen las comisiones». STEP 6: to say what something is for, use «para» + infinitive: «Necesito una tarjeta para pagar en tiendas». STEP 7: two false friends: «ingresar» means to deposit money (or to be admitted to an institution, such as a hospital); to walk into a bank, say «entrar en el banco». «Nómina» is your payslip and, in Spain, also your salary paid into the account. STEP 8: in Latin America some vocabulary changes: instead of «ingresar» you hear «depositar», instead of «sacar» also «retirar», and «cuenta corriente» or «cuenta de ahorros» appear more often.

"Fee" or "charge" at a bank is «comisión». "To deposit" is «ingresar» (Spain) or «depositar»; «ingresar» never means to walk in.

Contratar, reclamar e cancelar um serviç: Signing up for, complaining about and cancelling a service
PASSO 1: para contratar, use o imperfect: STEP 1: to sign up, use the polite imperfect or the conditional: «Quería contratar una línea» (I wanted to get a line), «Quisiera cambiar de tarifa». To ask for information, «Me gustaría saber si…» + indicative: «Me gustaría saber si hay cobertura en mi zona.» STEP 2: to describe something you're looking for and don't know exists, use the subjunctive: «Busco una tarifa que incluya muchos datos» (any one that would do). If you're describing something that exists, use the indicative: «Tengo una tarifa que incluye muchos datos». STEP 3: to say what has happened and still matters today, use the present perfect (lesson 17): «Me han cobrado dos veces la misma factura» (They've charged me twice for the same bill). STEP 4: to say how long a problem has been going on, use «llevar» + time + «sin» + noun or infinitive: «Llevo dos días sin cobertura» (I've had no signal for two days), «Llevo una semana sin recibir la factura». STEP 5: to ask them to fix it, use polite phrases: «¿Podrían revisar mi factura?» or «Quisiera que revisaran mi factura», with the imperfect subjunctive (lesson 46), which sounds softer than «quiero que revisen». STEP 6: to cancel, «darse de baja» means to cancel a service, and «darse de alta» means to sign up or register. You can also say «cancelar la línea». STEP 7: many providers have a minimum contract period (in Spain, «permanencia»); always ask: «¿El contrato tiene permanencia?». In many countries you can keep your number when you switch provider («portabilidad»), but the rules vary: check. STEP 8: false friend: «reclamar» means to demand something you're entitled to (not "reclaim"); to make a formal complaint, say «presentar una reclamación», and to complain about something, «quejarse de».
em português dizemos «estou há dois dias: English "I've had no signal for two days" uses a perfect; Spanish uses «llevar» + time + «sin»: «Llevo dos días sin cobertura», not «He tenido no cobertura». In casual speech you also hear «tengo dos días sin cobertura», but stick with «llevar». "To complain" is «quejarse» or «presentar una reclamación»; «reclamar» is to demand or claim back. And "the bill" for a service is «la factura» (in a restaurant it's «la cuenta»).

Perguntar e negociar condições do alugue: Asking about and negotiating rental conditions
AVISO: contratos, depósitos, prazos e di: NOTE: contracts, deposits, deadlines and tenants' rights vary a lot from place to place; get everything in writing and check the current rules. STEP 1: to ask what's included, use «estar incluido»: «¿Están incluidos los gastos?» (Are bills included?). Watch the agreement: «El agua está incluida» («agua» is feminine, even with «el»). STEP 2: to ask whether something is allowed, use «se» + verb: «¿Se admiten mascotas?» (Are pets allowed?), «¿Se puede fumar en el piso?». STEP 3: to set a condition, use «siempre que» + subjunctive (as long as): «Acepto el piso siempre que me lo dejen amueblado». STEP 4: to say what happens before an action, use «antes de» + infinitive: «Antes de firmar, quisiera leer el contrato». English "before signing" uses -ing; Spanish uses the infinitive. STEP 5: to say something should be in writing, use «por escrito»: «Prefiero tenerlo por escrito». STEP 6: vocabulary: in Spain, «piso» is a flat/apartment; in Latin America you hear «apartamento» or «departamento». «Alquilar» works for both tenant and landlord, just like English "rent": «alquilar un piso» (as a tenant) or «alquilar mi piso a alguien» (as the owner). «Fianza» is the deposit in Spain; in Latin America people also say «depósito» or «garantía».

Watch out: «piso» is a flat (or a storey), while the floor you walk on is «el suelo». And "I'm interested in" = «estoy interesado en», with «en», like English "in".
